headline: UN votes for a map that shows Africa at its true size

sources.title: UN votes to adopt a new world map that shows more accurately Africa's size (AP News)
UN tells the world: Stop making Africa look small (UN News)
The U.N. backs a new world map showing Africa in its true relative size (NPR)
The United Nations votes to adopt a new map that shows Africa's true scale (video, DW News)

chunks.text: The United Nations General Assembly voted on Friday, September 4, 2026, to encourage the world to {{move away from}} the [[traditional]] Mercator map. Togo {{put forward}} the [[resolution]] on behalf of the African Group, with the [[backing]] of the African Union. It {{went through}} with 164 votes [[in favor]]. The United States was the only country to vote against it, and six countries, including Ukraine and Serbia, [[abstained]].

verbs.wrong: To continue to the next topic
verbs.why: A city can move away from coal for its power, and a family can move away from paper bills. The UN resolution encourages the world to move away from the traditional Mercator map.

verbs.correct: To officially suggest for a vote
verbs.wrong: To delay until a later meeting
verbs.why: A council member can put forward a plan for a new park, and a student can put forward an idea at a club meeting. Togo put forward the resolution on behalf of the African Group.

verbs.correct: To be approved by a vote
verbs.wrong: To be debated for a long time
verbs.why: A new budget goes through when enough people vote for it, and a company deal goes through once the owners agree. The resolution went through with 164 votes in favor.

chunks.text: The Mercator map {{dates back}} to 1569, when a Flemish [[mapmaker]] named Mercator designed it for sailors. On his map, a straight line matches a fixed [[compass direction]], so [[navigators]] could {{map out}} a course along one straight line. The price was size. The map {{blows up}} [[landmasses]] near the [[poles]], so Greenland {{comes across as}} roughly the same size as Africa, although Africa is about 14 times larger.

verbs.correct: To have existed since a time
verbs.wrong: To be replaced by a newer version
verbs.why: A stone bridge can date back to Roman times, and a family recipe can date back to a grandmother. The Mercator map dates back to 1569, when it was designed for sailors.

verbs.correct: To plan a route in detail
verbs.wrong: To measure the size of land
verbs.why: A hiker maps out a trail the night before, and a delivery driver maps out the day's stops. On the Mercator map, navigators could map out a course along one straight line.

verbs.wrong: To copy onto a flat surface
verbs.why: A photo shop can blow up a small picture to poster size, and a phone screen blows up text when you zoom in. The Mercator map blows up landmasses near the poles.

verbs.correct: To seem to be a certain way
verbs.why: A quiet person can come across as unfriendly, and a short email can come across as rude. On the Mercator map, Greenland comes across as roughly the same size as Africa.

chunks.text: The Equal Earth [[projection]] is much newer. A former [[senior cartographer]] at the U.S. National Park Service {{came up with}} it in 2018 with two colleagues. It shows continents in their [[true proportions]], though shapes are slightly [[distorted]]. The resolution {{calls on}} governments, schools, international organizations and technology companies to use Equal Earth and similar maps when [[relative size]] matters. It is not [[binding]]. It does not ban Mercator and does not {{rule out}} its use for sea and air navigation.

verbs.why: A teacher can come up with a new game for class, and a friend can come up with a name for a cafe. A former senior cartographer at the U.S. National Park Service came up with the Equal Earth projection in 2018 with two colleagues.

verbs.correct: To formally ask someone to act
verbs.why: A mayor can call on residents to save water, and a coach can call on players to train harder. The resolution calls on governments, schools and technology companies to use Equal Earth.

verbs.correct: To say something is not allowed
verbs.wrong: To make a formal decision about
verbs.why: A school can rule out phones during exams, and a landlord can rule out pets in an apartment. The resolution does not rule out the use of Mercator for sea and air navigation.

chunks.text: Togo's [[foreign minister]] said, "Maps shape our understanding of the world." The United States {{spoke out against}} the resolution, calling it part of an [[ideological]] project. Ukraine raised concerns about how [[occupied territory]] would appear, and the European Union said the vote had no [[bearing]] on borders. France said it would {{switch over to}} Equal Earth for its world maps. Africa No Filter, a campaign group, wants accurate maps {{rolled out}} in schools, textbooks and news organizations.

verbs.wrong: To give the views of a group
verbs.why: Parents can speak out against a school closing, and workers can speak out against a pay cut. The United States spoke out against the resolution, calling it part of an ideological project.

verbs.correct: To change to a different one
verbs.why: A family can switch over to a cheaper phone plan, and an office can switch over to a new email system. France said it would switch over to Equal Earth for its world maps.

verbs.wrong: To return to an earlier version
verbs.why: A bank can roll out a new app to all its customers, and a city can roll out electric buses over a year. Africa No Filter, a campaign group, wants accurate maps rolled out in schools, textbooks and news organizations.

mainIdea.s: The UN General Assembly voted to encourage the Equal Earth map instead of the Mercator map, which makes Africa look much smaller than it is. The vote is a recommendation, not a ban.
mainIdea.why: Togo's resolution went through 164 to 1 and calls on governments, schools and companies to use Equal Earth, but it is not binding and does not ban Mercator.

mainIdea.s: UN members voted to ban the Mercator map from schools and government offices worldwide. Every country now has until the end of this year to switch to the Equal Earth projection.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the resolution only encourages the use of Equal Earth. It does not ban Mercator or impose a replacement, and it sets no deadline for anyone.

mainIdea.s: The African Union has launched its own online map service that shows the continent at its true size. Millions of people around the world downloaded the new app in its first week.
mainIdea.why: The African Union backed a UN vote on map projections. It did not launch a map service or an app.

tf.s: The United States was the only country that voted against the resolution.
tf.why: In all, 164 member states voted in favor and six abstained, and the United States spoke out against the resolution, calling it part of an ideological project.

tf.s: The resolution bans the Mercator map for sea and air navigation.
tf.why: The resolution is not binding, does not ban Mercator, and does not rule out its use for sea and air navigation.

tf.s: On the Mercator map, Greenland looks about the same size as Africa.
tf.why: The map blows up landmasses near the poles, although Africa is about 14 times larger than Greenland.

tf.s: The Equal Earth projection was created in 1569.
tf.why: A former senior cartographer at the U.S. National Park Service and two colleagues came up with Equal Earth in 2018; it is the Mercator map that dates back to 1569.

tf.s: Togo put the resolution forward on behalf of the African Group.
tf.why: Togo had the backing of the African Union, and the resolution went through with 164 votes in favor.

tf.s: France said it would keep using the Mercator map for its world maps.
tf.why: France said it would switch over to Equal Earth for its world maps.

lines.text: Did you see the UN vote on the world map? It {{went through}} on Friday, 164 to 1.
The Mercator thing? I saw something about Africa and Greenland.
Right. On the Mercator map, Greenland {{comes across as}} about the same size as Africa. Africa is actually 14 times larger.
Fourteen times? [[I had no idea]]. Why is the map so wrong?
It {{dates back}} to 1569. Mercator designed it for sailors, so they could {{map out}} a route as a straight line. The trade is that it {{blows up}} everything near the poles.
So it was never meant for classroom walls.
Not really. A geography professor at Syracuse said that outside navigation there is no point in using it.
[[Old habits die hard]], I guess. What did the UN actually decide?
Togo {{put forward}} a resolution that {{calls on}} governments, schools and tech companies to {{move away from}} Mercator and use Equal Earth instead.
Yes. A former senior cartographer at the U.S. National Park Service {{came up with}} it with two colleagues. It keeps sizes right, though the shapes are a little distorted.
And is anyone forced to change?

No, it isn't binding. It doesn't even {{rule out}} Mercator for navigation. But France says it will {{switch over to}} Equal Earth, and the campaign groups want accurate maps {{rolled out}} in schools and textbooks.

Only the United States. Its representative {{spoke out against}} it and called it an ideological project. Six countries abstained, including Ukraine, which was worried about how occupied territory would look.
[[You can see their point]]. Still, [[it's a start]].
I liked one line from Togo's foreign minister: a fair map doesn't change the world's geography, it changes how we see it.
